title: Frame the Technical Problem
goal: Turn the system context into a framed technical problem: solution-free, with ranked unknowns, measurable targets and a spike plan.

processes.title: Frame the Technical Problem
processes.summary: Separate the problem from the proposed solution, list the unknowns as hypotheses, set measurable quality targets and plan time-boxed spikes.

definition.purpose: Turn the system context into a framed technical problem: solution-free, with ranked unknowns, measurable targets and a spike plan.
definition.outcome: A technical framing pack the tech lead accepts: the problem split from the proposal, ranked hypotheses, quality targets and spikes.
definition.jtbd: When I understand the system, help me frame the problem so the investigation answers the questions that matter.

definition.purpose: Stop the first solution anyone mentioned from becoming the design, by stating the technical problem on its own.

workflows.title: Split Problem from Solution
workflows.summary: Record the proposed solution exactly, ladder down to the failure it is meant to fix, and state that failure without naming any technology.

steps.title: Record the proposed solution as asked
steps.ask: From the brief and my notes, write down every solution anyone has proposed, word for word, with who proposed it. Don't judge or rephrase them yet.

lenses.note: Record the proposal exactly — it becomes an option, not the plan.

steps.title: Ladder from the solution to the failure
steps.ask: For the main proposal, build a why-chain: ask what it's for, then why that matters, one line at a time, until you reach a condition in the system (cite SYS / DF IDs from my system context pack). Stop when no tool or product is named.

lenses.note: Keep asking why until a system condition appears.
Note when the proposal is 'use AI' — the problem is what AI would fix.

steps.title: State the problem without solution words
steps.ask: State the problem in two or three sentences with no technology, product or vendor named — what fails, where in the flow, and what would show it's fixed. Then list the original proposal as one option for later.

lenses.note: No technology or product in the problem.
Cite the data flows where it fails.

steps.title: Problem stated without a solution?
steps.ask: Check my problem statement for hidden solution words and anything not supported by the system context pack, so I can take it to the tech lead.

lenses.note: Would two engineers read this the same way?

contract.definition: Record the proposed solution exactly, ladder down to the failure it is meant to fix, and state that failure without naming any technology.
decisions: Is the problem stated without a solution?
failures: The proposed tool is restated as the problem
recovery: Ask 'what goes wrong today without it?' until no tool is named
Restore the verbatim proposal from the brief
exit: Problem agreed with the tech lead
contract.handoff: Problem / solution split → 1.2.2 List Unknowns & Technical Hypotheses
traceability: Problem links to SYS-##, DF-## and REQ-###
learning: Proposals that hid a different problem — learning log

objectives: Record a proposed solution without adopting it
Ladder from the solution to the failure it fixes
lessons.exercise: Write a why-chain from “use AI to read the PDFs” down to a system condition, then state the problem with no technology named. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: When do you stop asking why?
options: When you reach a condition in the system, not a tool
quiz.why: Stop at a system condition you can measure.

lessons.title: List Unknowns & Technical Hypotheses
lessons.summary: Turn what you don't know into falsifiable technical hypotheses, ranked by risk.

definition.purpose: Make every technical unknown explicit and testable, so discovery spends its time on the riskiest ones.
definition.outcome: A ranked list of technical hypotheses, each with how it could be proved wrong.
definition.jtbd: Help me know what could sink this technically, and which question to answer first.
exit: Every unknown written as a falsifiable hypothesis
Top three risks agreed with the tech lead

normal: Collect unknowns from the question and constraint logs
Write each as a falsifiable hypothesis
Rate impact and uncertainty
Rank and agree the top three
parallel: Ranking runs as hypotheses are written

cases.happyPath: A handful of clear hypotheses, with two or three that obviously matter most.
alternates: Very few unknowns → rank them and move straight to spikes
edgeCases: An unknown can only be answered in production → find the nearest safe proxy
exceptions: Two hypotheses contradict each other → keep both; the spike decides

routing.forward: Ranked hypotheses → 1.2.3 Set Quality Attributes & Success Metrics
routing.alternate: Well-understood problem → short list, no ranking workshop
routing.escalation: Disagreement on the top risks → tech lead decides
routing.stop: No real unknowns → skip to quality attributes and record why — recorded in the learning log

criteria: Each hypothesis says what result would prove it wrong
Each has impact and uncertainty rated
checks: Tech lead agrees the top three
policies: Assumptions from the constraint log are carried, not dropped

concerns: Spending discovery on the easy questions

agents: AI coding agent for drafting hypotheses

continuity.handoff: Technical hypothesis list → 1.2.3 Set Quality Attributes & Success Metrics
traceability: Creates H-## linked to Q-## or A-##
learning: Riskiest unknowns in hindsight — learning log

workflows.title: Rank the Unknowns
workflows.summary: Collect every open technical question and assumption, write each as a hypothesis that could be proved wrong, and rank them by impact and uncertainty.

steps.title: Collect unknowns from the logs
steps.ask: Collect every open question from my question log and every low- or medium-confidence assumption from my constraint log into one list.

lenses.note: Every open question and low-confidence assumption.

steps.title: Write each as a falsifiable hypothesis
steps.ask: Rewrite each unknown as a hypothesis — 'We believe … ; we're wrong if …' — with a concrete result that would prove it wrong. One unknown per hypothesis.

lenses.note: Each says what result proves it wrong.

steps.title: Rate impact & uncertainty
steps.ask: Rate each hypothesis on impact (how badly it would hurt if wrong) and uncertainty (how little evidence we have), rank them, and say how each could be tested: spike, measure, ask or docs.

lenses.note: Volume and speed unknowns rated honestly.
Security unknowns aren't left to the end.
Data-quality unknowns rated by impact.

steps.title: Riskiest unknowns agreed?
steps.ask: Prepare the top three hypotheses for the tech lead with a one-line case for why each could sink the build.

lenses.note: Are the top three the ones that could change the architecture?

contract.definition: Collect every open technical question and assumption, write each as a hypothesis that could be proved wrong, and rank them by impact and uncertainty.
recovery: Add 'we are wrong if…' to each
contract.handoff: Technical hypothesis list → 1.2.3 Set Quality Attributes & Success Metrics
traceability: H-## links to Q-## or A-##
learning: Unknowns that turned out to matter most — learning log

lessons.exercise: Write three hypotheses for the order-intake case, each with 'we're wrong if…', and rank them. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: Which unknowns do you test first?
quiz.why: They are the ones that could sink the build.

lessons.title: Set Quality Attributes & Success Metrics
lessons.summary: Decide which quality attributes matter most and how technical success will be measured.

definition.purpose: Make 'good enough' measurable before any option is compared, so the choice is judged against agreed targets.
definition.outcome: Ranked quality attributes and technical success metrics with targets and how each is measured.
definition.jtbd: Help me know what the solution must be good at, in numbers, before I pick one.
exit: Every metric has a target and a way to measure it

normal: Shortlist quality attributes from ISO/IEC 25010
Rank them for this problem
Write each as a measurable scenario
Set the success metrics and targets
Agree with the tech lead
parallel: Scenarios are written while metrics are set

cases.happyPath: Two or three attributes clearly matter most and each has a number.
alternates: Targets unknown → set a provisional target and mark it to confirm with the baseline
edgeCases: Two attributes conflict (e.g. accuracy vs latency) → record the trade-off
exceptions: A target is set by regulation → it is a hard constraint

routing.forward: Quality priorities & metrics → 1.2.4 Plan Time-boxed Discovery Spikes
routing.alternate: Small change → one attribute, one metric
routing.escalation: Attributes conflict beyond the team → tech lead and client
routing.stop: Nothing measurable → stop and say what's missing — recorded in the learning log

criteria: Every metric has a number, a unit and a measurement method
policies: Regulatory targets confirmed by their owner

decisions: What must the solution be good at, in numbers?

agents: AI coding agent for drafting scenarios
execution.authority: Tech lead agrees the targets; the client confirms business-facing numbers.

continuity.handoff: Quality priorities & success metrics → 1.2.4 Plan Time-boxed Discovery Spikes
traceability: Creates QA-## and M-## linked to H-##

workflows.title: Set Quality Targets
workflows.summary: Rank the ISO/IEC 25010 quality attributes that matter for this problem, write each as a measurable scenario and set the technical success metrics.

steps.title: Rank the quality attributes
steps.ask: From ISO/IEC 25010, shortlist the quality attributes that matter for this problem and rank them — at most three at the top — with one line on why each matters here.

lenses.note: Rank — not everything can be top priority.

steps.title: Write each as a measurable scenario
steps.ask: Write each top attribute as a scenario: 'When [stimulus], the system [response], measured as [number]'. Use the volumes and limits from my system context pack.

lenses.note: Latency and throughput as numbers at peak.
What must never be lost, and recovery time.
Security expectations stated, not assumed.

steps.title: Set success metrics & targets
steps.ask: Define the technical success metrics: name, target, how and where it will be measured, and which quality attribute it proves. Mark baselines as 'to measure' where we don't have them yet.

lenses.note: Every target says how it will be tested.

steps.title: Targets measurable?
steps.ask: Check every target is a number with a unit and a measurement method, and flag any two that conflict.

lenses.note: Every target measurable and agreed.

contract.definition: Rank the ISO/IEC 25010 quality attributes that matter for this problem, write each as a measurable scenario and set the technical success metrics.
recovery: Force a ranking — at most three at the top
Add how and where each is measured
contract.handoff: Quality priorities & success metrics → 1.2.4 Plan Time-boxed Discovery Spikes
traceability: QA-## and M-## link to H-## and REQ-###
learning: Targets that moved later — learning log

objectives: Write each as a measurable scenario
lessons.exercise: Write the reliability scenario for the order-intake case: when…, the system…, measured as…. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: “The system must be fast.” What's missing?
options: A number, a load and how it's measured
quiz.why: Targets need numbers and a method.

lessons.title: Plan Time-boxed Discovery Spikes
lessons.summary: Turn the riskiest hypotheses into small, time-boxed experiments with a clear success signal.

definition.purpose: Spend discovery effort only where it buys the most certainty, in fixed time-boxes.
definition.outcome: A spike plan: each spike tied to a hypothesis, with approach, timebox, success signal and owner — and the framing pack handed on.
definition.jtbd: Help me plan the smallest experiments that answer the questions that could sink this.
exit: Each top hypothesis has a spike or a reason it needs none

normal: Pick the hypotheses that need a spike
Design the smallest test for each
Set a timebox and a success signal
Assemble the framing pack
Tech lead approval

cases.happyPath: Two or three spikes, each a day or less, each answering one hypothesis.
alternates: Hypothesis answerable from docs → answer it, no spike
edgeCases: Spike needs production data → use a masked sample or synthetic data
exceptions: Spike needs a paid service → use the free tier or a trial
failures: A spike can't be designed inside any timebox

routing.forward: Framing pack & spike plan → 1.3 Investigate the Real Problem
routing.alternate: No spike needed → record why and move on
routing.escalation: Spike needs money or access → tech lead
routing.stop: Nothing worth testing → stop framing and record why — recorded in the learning log

criteria: Every spike has a timebox and a success signal set in advance
rules: Spikes are throwaway — no spike code goes to production

principles: Learn the most for the least

agents: AI coding agent for scaffolding spikes
execution.authority: Tech lead approves the spike plan and its timeboxes.

continuity.handoff: Technical framing pack & spike plan → 1.3 Investigate the Real Problem
learning: Spikes that ran over — learning log

workflows.title: Plan the Spikes
workflows.summary: For each risky hypothesis, design the smallest time-boxed experiment that could prove it wrong, with the success signal set before it runs.

steps.title: Pick hypotheses that need a spike
steps.ask: From my ranked hypotheses, pick the ones a spike can answer. For the rest, say how they'll be answered instead (docs, a measurement, asking an owner).

uses.name: Learn the most for the least
uses.ref: Learn the most for the least

lenses.note: Only hypotheses that a spike can answer.

steps.title: Design the smallest test for each
steps.ask: For each, design the smallest throwaway test that could prove the hypothesis wrong — what to build or run, on which data and environment. No production systems.

lenses.note: Test environments and trial accounts named.
Masked or synthetic data only.
Accuracy measured on our own samples.

steps.title: Set timebox & success signal
steps.ask: Give each spike a timebox (a day or less unless justified) and a success signal written now, before any result exists.

lenses.note: Success signal set before running.

steps.title: Assemble the framing pack
steps.ask: Assemble my technical framing pack: one paragraph each for the problem, the ranked unknowns, the quality targets and the spike plan, with links to the full documents.

lenses.note: Pack reads as one frame.

steps.title: Spike plan approved?
steps.ask: Review my spike plan as the tech lead would: is every spike small, time-boxed, safe and tied to one hypothesis?

lenses.note: Is every spike small enough?
Nothing touches production.

loops: Needs money or access → tech lead

contract.definition: For each risky hypothesis, design the smallest time-boxed experiment that could prove it wrong, with the success signal set before it runs.
failures: Success signal set after the result
recovery: Cap every spike at a day unless the tech lead agrees more
Write the signal into the plan before starting
criteria: Timebox and signal set in advance
contract.handoff: Technical framing pack & spike plan → 1.3 Investigate the Real Problem
learning: Spikes that ran over — learning log

objectives: Design the smallest test for a hypothesis
Set a timebox and success signal in advance
lessons.exercise: Write SPK-1 for OCR accuracy: test, timebox, success signal and data. Then do the same for your own project.

quiz.q: Can spike code go to production if it works?
options: No — spikes are throwaway; build it properly later
quiz.why: Spike code is built to learn, not to last.
